asr_transcript: Calibration asks a simulation to match selected observations at a starting point. Validation asks whether it predicts change away from that point. This paper tests illustrious TNG from the local universe toward Redshift's 4-6 using SDSS and JWST. The test follows two galaxy relationships at fixed stellar mass. The star-forming main sequence tracks how quickly galaxies make stars. The mass-metallicity relation tracks their oxygen abundance. Each population is compared with the observed local relation. Two numbers must stay separate. First is each population's position relative to the observed local SDSS relation. Second is TNG's change relative to its own Redshift zero relation. Only the second cancels TNG's local calibration error and fairly tests evolution. At Redshift zero, before any evolution is measured, TNG already starts in the wrong places. Its star-forming main sequence is 3-tenths of a dex below SDSS, while its mass-metallicity relation is about 1200s of a dex above. A raw comparison can look reassuring because TNG starts low. After that starting residual is removed, its main sequence growth reaches about 1.3 to 1.6 Observed galaxies rise only about 0.9 to 1.0 dex. Metallicity is harder because the three data sets do not begin on one measurement scale. SDSS used a calibration that runs roughly 2 to 3-tenths of a dex above direct electron temperature values. TNG also converts total metal fraction using a fixed solar ratio. After placing the comparisons on one electron temperature anchored scale, the observed high Redshift metallicity deficit is about 0.4 dex. TNG decreases by about 0.27 dex. That gap is within the remaining calibration systematic, so it is not significant. The reproducible mismatch is over-strong star formation growth. Metallicity remains scale-limited. Selection, stellar mass definitions, apertures, and a small Redshift 6 sample still matter. This machine-generated draft is descriptive, not validated.
